rationale: Randomized 4-week trial in 80 menopausal women of tablets made from freshly harvested Salvia officinalis extract (3,400 mg tincture equivalent), not fresh culinary leaf and not PD. Full body reports lower fatigue and physical/mental exhaustion; fatigue questionnaire difference vs placebo p=.029, but arm-specific values are ambiguously presented and cannot be safely assigned.

Review body mentions fatigue as a generic menopause symptom; its Salvia-specific discussion concerns estrogenic assays and hot flashes, not a measured fatigue outcome or a tested fresh-leaf intervention.

Randomized crossover exercise study in athletes (26 enrolled, 17 analyzed): 400 mg aqueous Salvia officinalis leaf extract plus 200 mg Salvia lavandulaefolia essential oil in a capsule, 2 hours pre-exercise. Rating of perceived exertion was lower with supplement (0.3 points; 95% CI 0.1–0.5; p=.002); exertional perception, not clinical fatigue severity, and not PD.

Abstract reports a balanced crossover in 36 healthy adults: single 50 µL oral Salvia lavandulaefolia essential-oil capsule vs placebo; mental fatigue decreased and alertness increased, more at 4 h. Spanish sage essential oil and healthy cognition, not fresh culinary sage or PD fatigue. Full article not verified accessible.
Network-pharmacology and docking study based on databases; no administered sage, human participants, or fatigue outcome.
Review of phytocompounds and neuroprotection; sage appears among botanicals, but no isolated sage exposure or fatigue endpoint is reported in the indexed abstract.
Computational QSAR/docking study includes sage-derived compounds among screened ligands; no consumed sage and no fatigue measure.

Full preprint is computational network pharmacology/docking only, with no administered sage or fatigue outcome. Same title/authors and study as PMID40266402 journal publication; count as a preprint/journal version pair, not independent evidence.

Full review cites the same 36-person Spanish-sage essential-oil crossover (PMID20937617) for reduced mental fatigue/increased alertness; this is a secondary account of that one study, not an independent cohort or PD fatigue result.

Abstract describes oral rosmarinic acid 20 mg/kg by gavage for 14 days in an MPTP mouse model; reports hyperlocomotion and neurotransmission outcomes, not fatigue. Isolated constituent/preclinical context only, not a sage-food intervention.

Full essential-oil neurodegeneration review body has no fatigue discussion; it reports biochemical/preclinical evidence and says human studies were not included in its search. No measured fatigue outcome or relevant food exposure.
